claim: FoxO blocks proliferation and progression in mTORC1-driven tumorigenesis.
source: The transcription factor FoxO has been shown to block proliferation and progression in mTORC1-driven tumorigenesis but the picture of the relevant FoxO target genes remains incomplete.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work establishing this relationship.

claim: Endoplasmic reticulum-associated protein degradation pathway components are downregulated upon foxo knockdown in Tsc1-deficient cells under nutrient restriction.
source: Transcriptomics analysis revealed downregulation of endoplasmic reticulum-associated protein degradation pathway components upon foxo knockdown.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq transcriptomics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pharmacological induction of ER stress enhances overgrowth of Tsc1 knockdown tissue.
source: Induction of ER stress pharmacologically or by suppression of other ER stress response pathway components led to an enhanced overgrowth of Tsc1 knockdown tissue.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using small molecule inhibitors.

claim: Suppression of ER stress response pathway components enhances overgrowth of Tsc1 knockdown tissue.
source: Induction of ER stress pharmacologically or by suppression of other ER stress response pathway components led to an enhanced overgrowth of Tsc1 knockdown tissue.
evidence: Supported by genetic manipulation experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: ER stress is increased in Tsc1 loss-of-function cells upon foxo knockdown.
source: Increase of ER stress in Tsc1 loss-of-function cells upon foxo knockdown was also confirmed by elevated expression levels of known ER stress markers.
evidence: Supported by expression data of ER stress markers.

claim: FoxO limits ER stress to regulate Tsc1 mutant overgrowth.
source: These results highlight the role of FoxO in limiting ER stress to regulate Tsc1 mutant overgrowth.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results showing FoxO's effect on ER stress and growth.

claim: The PI3K/Akt/mTORC1 network is the central regulator of cell growth, survival, and metabolism.
source: The phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt/mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) network is the central regulator of cell growth, survival, and metabolism (Manning and Toker, 2017; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: mTORC1 integrates growth factor signaling via Akt with intracellular nutrient and energy status to promote anabolism and suppress catabolic processes.
source: mTORC1 integrates growth factor signaling via Akt with the intracellular nutrient and energy status to promote anabolism and suppress catabolic processes (Ben-Sahra and Manning, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Deregulation of the PI3K/Akt/mTORC1 network leads to human cancers.
source: The key regulatory function of the network is highlighted by its deregulation leading to human cancers (Zhang et al., 2017), and the evolutionary conservation across organisms including Drosophila melanogaster (Engelman et al., 2006; Katewa and Kapahi, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on cancer biology.

claim: The PI3K/Akt/mTORC1 network is evolutionarily conserved across organisms including Drosophila melanogaster.
source: The key regulatory function of the network is highlighted by its deregulation leading to human cancers (Zhang et al., 2017), and the evolutionary conservation across organisms including Drosophila melanogaster (Engelman et al., 2006; Katewa and Kapahi, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to comparative biology literature.

claim: Pten and the tuberous sclerosis complex proteins Tsc1 and Tsc2 are major tumor suppressors in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, the major tumor suppressors of this network are phosphatase and tensin homolog (Pten) and the tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) proteins Tsc1 and Tsc2.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge in Drosophila genetics.

claim: Pten counteracts PI3K function by dephosphorylating PIP3 to PIP2.
source: Pten counteracts the function of PI3K by dephosphorylating the second messenger phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-triphosphate (PIP3) to phosphatidylinositol-4,5-biphosphate (PIP2) (Klippel et al., 1997), thereby inhibiting Akt activity (Goberdhan et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to biochemical studies.

claim: Pten inhibits Akt activity by dephosphorylating PIP3 to PIP2.
source: Pten counteracts the function of PI3K by dephosphorylating the second messenger phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-triphosphate (PIP3) to phosphatidylinositol-4,5-biphosphate (PIP2) (Klippel et al., 1997), thereby inhibiting Akt activity (Goberdhan et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to signaling pathway studies.

claim: The TSC complex inactivates mTORC1 downstream of Akt via its GTPase activating protein activity towards Rheb.
source: The TSC complex inactivates mTORC1 downstream of Akt (Potter et al., 2002) via its GTPase activating protein (GAP) activity towards Rheb (Saucedo et al., 2003; Stocker et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: FoxO is a major downstream target of Akt.
source: Another major downstream target of Akt is the transcription factor Forkhead box O (FoxO) (Jünger et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to signaling pathway literature.

claim: The role of FoxO as a bona fide tumor suppressor is not established since it can function as tumor-promoting depending on biological context.
source: However, the role of FoxO as a bona fide tumor suppressor is not established since it can also function as tumor-promoting depending on the biological context (van Doeselaar and Burgering, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to review literature on FoxO function.

claim: Loss of Tsc1 leads to enhanced overgrowth of eye imaginal discs in larvae raised under nutrient restriction.
source: Using an early tumorigenesis model in Drosophila, we have shown that the loss of Tsc1 leads to an enhanced overgrowth of eye imaginal discs in larvae raised under nutrient restriction (NR) (Nowak et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Tsc1 loss-induced overgrowth is primarily hypertrophic in nature.
source: This overgrowth is primarily hypertrophic in nature.
evidence: Supported by prior characterization cited in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of Tsc1 induces hyperactivation of mTORC1 and an S6K-dependent negative feedback to insulin signaling.
source: Loss of Tsc1 induces hyperactivation of mTORC1 and an S6K-dependent negative feedback to insulin signaling.
evidence: Supported by established signaling pathway knowledge and prior work.

claim: Loss of Tsc1 causes downregulation of Akt and increased nuclear localization of FoxO, resulting in growth inhibition.
source: This causes downregulation of Akt and an increased nuclear localization of FoxO, resulting in growth inhibition.
evidence: Inferred from the signaling pathway relationships described.

claim: Suppression of FoxO function in Tsc1 mutant cells results in massively overgrown tissues that show ectopic differentiation.
source: Suppression of FoxO function in Tsc1 mutant cells results in massively overgrown tissues that show ectopic differentiation, demonstrating a role of FoxO in regulating proliferation and differentiation of these hyperactive mTORC1 cells.
evidence: Supported by prior experimental work cited in the manuscript.

claim: FoxO regulates proliferation and differentiation of hyperactive mTORC1 cells.
source: Suppression of FoxO function in Tsc1 mutant cells results in massively overgrown tissues that show ectopic differentiation, demonstrating a role of FoxO in regulating proliferation and differentiation of these hyperactive mTORC1 cells.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental phenotypes described.

claim: The Drosophila eye imaginal disc is composed of different populations of mitotically active and differentiating cells.
source: The Drosophila eye imaginal disc is composed of different populations of mitotically active and differentiating cells.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Drosophila developmental biology.

claim: Investigation for FoxO targets is required to be performed in specific cells under conditions being studied due to context and cell-type specificity of FoxO.
source: Given the context and cell-type specificity of FoxO (Webb et al., 2016), investigation for its targets is required to be performed in specific cells under conditions being studied.
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on FoxO specificity and logical inference.

claim: Laser capture microdissection has emerged as a useful tool for isolation of distinct cells of interest.
source: The laser capture microdissection (LCM) technique has emerged as a useful tool for isolation of distinct cells of interest (Iyer and Cox, 2010; Vicidomini et al., 2010) but a comprehensive analytical study has not been described previously in Drosophila.
evidence: Supported by citations to technical literature.

claim: A comprehensive analytical study using laser capture microdissection has not been described previously in Drosophila.
source: The laser capture microdissection (LCM) technique has emerged as a useful tool for isolation of distinct cells of interest (Iyer and Cox, 2010; Vicidomini et al., 2010) but a comprehensive analytical study has not been described previously in Drosophila.
evidence: Based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Downregulation of ER stress is a key mechanism downstream of FoxO to inhibit Tsc1 mutant overgrowth under nutrient restriction.
source: Our results identify downregulation of ER stress as a key mechanism downstream of FoxO to inhibit Tsc1 mutant overgrowth under NR.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A 12 hr shift to restrictive temperature is sufficient to achieve adequate foxo knockdown in Tsc1 mutant cells.
source: Evaluating the nuclear FoxO antibody staining in Tsc1 mutant cells (Manning et al., 2005) in time-course experiments revealed that a 12 hr shift was sufficient to achieve an adequate foxo knockdown (Figure 1B and B').
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B and B'.

claim: Knockdown of foxo for a short duration limits the detection of secondary transcriptional targets.
source: The knockdown of foxo for a short duration limited the detection of secondary transcriptional targets, as illustrated earlier (Gan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work and logical inference about experimental design.

claim: 24 genes are downregulated in Tsc1 mutant cells upon foxo knockdown under nutrient restriction.
source: Differential gene expression analysis of Tsc1 mutant cells, with or without foxo knockdown, under NR revealed 24 downregulated and 128 upregulated genes (ANOVA, logFC > 0.8 and FDR < 0.2, Figure 1C) in the absence of foxo.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 128 genes are upregulated in Tsc1 mutant cells upon foxo knockdown under nutrient restriction.
source: Differential gene expression analysis of Tsc1 mutant cells, with or without foxo knockdown, under NR revealed 24 downregulated and 128 upregulated genes (ANOVA, logFC > 0.8 and FDR < 0.2, Figure 1C) in the absence of foxo.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Downregulated genes in Tsc1 mutant cells upon foxo knockdown are enriched in biological processes such as protein deglycosylation, protein refolding, and protein localization to ER.
source: Gene Ontology analysis of the downregulated genes showed enrichment in various biological processes such as protein deglycosylation, protein refolding, and protein localization to ER (Figure 1C'), and these genes have been further validated (see below).
evidence: Supported by Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 1C'.

claim: More than half of the 128 upregulated genes code for small nucleolar RNAs and associated small nuclear RNAs.
source: From the 128 upregulated genes, more than half code for small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs), and associated small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs).
evidence: Supported by analysis of the RNA-seq data.

claim: CG6766 is the top candidate gene that enhances Tsc1 mutant overgrowth when knocked down.
source: The top candidate from all genetic tests was the uncharacterized gene CG6766, encoding an ortholog of the mammalian endoplasmic reticulum lectin 1 (ERLEC1).
evidence: Supported by in vivo RNAi screening data presented in Figure 2.

claim: CG6766 encodes an ortholog of mammalian endoplasmic reticulum lectin 1 (ERLEC1).
source: The top candidate from all genetic tests was the uncharacterized gene CG6766, encoding an ortholog of the mammalian endoplasmic reticulum lectin 1 (ERLEC1).
evidence: Based on sequence homology and established orthology relationships.

claim: CG6766 is predicted to localize to ER/Golgi.
source: It is predicted to localize to ER/Golgi and is considered to be a component of the ubiquitin-dependent ERAD pathway (Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to computational prediction study.

claim: CG6766 is considered to be a component of the ubiquitin-dependent ERAD pathway.
source: It is predicted to localize to ER/Golgi and is considered to be a component of the ubiquitin-dependent ERAD pathway (Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to pathway analysis study.

claim: CG8860 is involved in protein processing in the ER.
source: Another candidate that is involved in protein processing in the ER, CG8860, also scored positively in the in vivo assays, suggesting a role for ER homeostasis in determining Tsc1 mutant overgrowth.
evidence: Based on known function and in vivo assay results.

claim: CG8860 is orthologous to mammalian SEC61 translocon gamma subunit (SEC61G).
source: CG8860 is orthologous to the mammalian SEC61 translocon gamma subunit (SEC61G).
evidence: Based on sequence homology and established orthology relationships.

claim: ER homeostasis plays a role in determining Tsc1 mutant overgrowth.
source: Another candidate that is involved in protein processing in the ER, CG8860, also scored positively in the in vivo assays, suggesting a role for ER homeostasis in determining Tsc1 mutant overgrowth.
evidence: Inferred from the positive results of multiple ER-related genes in the assays.

claim: Homozygous CG6766 mutant clones show similar calnexin staining patterns compared to surrounding wild-type tissue and isogenic control clones.
source: Homozygous mutant clones showed similar staining patterns compared to the surrounding wild-type tissue and the isogenic control clones (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression levels of spliced-Xbp1 are elevated in Tsc1 knockdown backgrounds upon knockdown of CG6766.
source: Quantitative reverse-transcription PCR (RT-qPCR) analysis on eye imaginal discs revealed no change in the expression levels of spliced-Xbp1 or Hsc-70–3 in the wild-type background upon knockdown of CG6766. By contrast, the expression levels of both ER stress reporters were elevated in Tsc1 knockdown backgrounds (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that CG6766 is limiting to maintain ER homeostasis in Tsc1 mutant cells.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression levels of Hsc-70–3 are elevated in Tsc1 knockdown backgrounds upon knockdown of CG6766.
source: Quantitative reverse-transcription PCR (RT-qPCR) analysis on eye imaginal discs revealed no change in the expression levels of spliced-Xbp1 or Hsc-70–3 in the wild-type background upon knockdown of CG6766. By contrast, the expression levels of both ER stress reporters were elevated in Tsc1 knockdown backgrounds (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that CG6766 is limiting to maintain ER homeostasis in Tsc1 mutant cells.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: CG6766 is limiting to maintain ER homeostasis in Tsc1 mutant cells.
source: Quantitative reverse-transcription PCR (RT-qPCR) analysis on eye imaginal discs revealed no change in the expression levels of spliced-Xbp1 or Hsc-70–3 in the wild-type background upon knockdown of CG6766. By contrast, the expression levels of both ER stress reporters were elevated in Tsc1 knockdown backgrounds (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that CG6766 is limiting to maintain ER homeostasis in Tsc1 mutant cells.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects in wild-type versus Tsc1 mutant backgrounds.

claim: The lack of ER stress response in cells mutant for CG6766 suggests a redundant function.
source: The lack of ER stress response in cells mutant for CG6766 suggests a (partially) redundant function, and may also explain why CG6766 (as well as CG8860) has not been characterized so far.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: Knockdown of several ERAD pathway components leads to an increase in Tsc1 knockdown eye size.
source: Knockdown of several ERAD pathway components led to an increase in Tsc1 knockdown eye size (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by in vivo RNAi screening data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Inhibition of core components of the ubiquitin ligase complex results in enlargement of Tsc1 knockdown eye size.
source: Particularly, inhibition of the core components of the ubiquitin ligase complex and those involved in the retrotranslocation of terminally misfolded proteins from ER to cytosol resulted in an enlargement of eye size.
evidence: Supported by in vivo RNAi screening data.

claim: Inhibition of components involved in retrotranslocation of terminally misfolded proteins from ER to cytosol results in enlargement of Tsc1 knockdown eye size.
source: Particularly, inhibition of the core components of the ubiquitin ligase complex and those involved in the retrotranslocation of terminally misfolded proteins from ER to cytosol resulted in an enlargement of eye size.
evidence: Supported by in vivo RNAi screening data.

claim: CG13426 encodes an ortholog of SEC61G similar to CG8860.
source: Of note, CG13426, which encodes an ortholog of SEC61G similar to the candidate from the transcriptomics analysis, CG8860, also led to an enhancement of the Tsc1 knockdown overgrowth.
evidence: Based on sequence homology and established orthology relationships.

claim: CG13426 knockdown leads to enhancement of Tsc1 knockdown overgrowth.
source: Of note, CG13426, which encodes an ortholog of SEC61G similar to the candidate from the transcriptomics analysis, CG8860, also led to an enhancement of the Tsc1 knockdown overgrowth.
evidence: Supported by in vivo RNAi screening data.

claim: A reduced efficiency of ERAD lowers the capacity of the ER to remove misfolded proteins.
source: A reduced efficiency of ERAD lowers the capacity of the ER to remove misfolded proteins.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ERAD function.

claim: In mammals, accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER causes activation of three signal transduction pathways: PERK, IRE1α and ATF6, together referred to as the unfolded protein response (UPR).
source: In mammals, accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER causes activation of the three signal transduction pathways: PERK, IRE1α and ATF6, together referred to as the unfolded protein response (UPR) (Wang and Kaufman, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to review literature on UPR.

claim: UPR pathways signal to induce apoptosis in case of chronic ER stress or maintain ER homeostasis by upregulating expression of several ERAD pathway genes.
source: These signal to induce apoptosis in case of chronic ER stress, or maintain ER homeostasis by upregulating expression of several ERAD pathway genes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of UPR function.

claim: The ERAD pathway links the ubiquitin-proteasome system to ER protein quality control as its substrates are transported into the cytosol for degradation by the proteasome.
source: The ERAD pathway also links the ubiquitin-proteasome system to ER protein quality control as its substrates are transported into the cytosol for degradation by the proteasome (Ruggiano et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to review literature on ERAD.

claim: Knockdown of UPR pathway genes does not display a consistent effect on Tsc1 knockdown overgrowth.
source: Knockdown of UPR or proteasomal degradation pathway genes did not display a consistent effect on Tsc1 knockdown overgrowth (Figure 3C and D), indicating that the effects might be specific to ERAD or that the manipulations are detrimental (proteasomal degradation pathway components).
evidence: Supported by in vivo RNAi screening data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Knockdown of proteasomal degradation pathway genes does not display a consistent effect on Tsc1 knockdown overgrowth.
source: Knockdown of UPR or proteasomal degradation pathway genes did not display a consistent effect on Tsc1 knockdown overgrowth (Figure 3C and D), indicating that the effects might be specific to ERAD or that the manipulations are detrimental (proteasomal degradation pathway components).
evidence: Supported by in vivo RNAi screening data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The effects of ERAD component knockdown on Tsc1 mutant overgrowth might be specific to ERAD.
source: Knockdown of UPR or proteasomal degradation pathway genes did not display a consistent effect on Tsc1 knockdown overgrowth (Figure 3C and D), indicating that the effects might be specific to ERAD or that the manipulations are detrimental (proteasomal degradation pathway components).
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on comparison of different pathway manipulations.

claim: Tunicamycin inhibits N-linked glycosylation and causes ER stress.
source: The inhibition of N-linked glycosylation by Tunicamycin (Kuo and Lampen, 1974), Ca2+ ATPase by Thapsigargin (Lytton et al., 1991), proteasome by MG132 (Lee and Goldberg, 1998), and ERAD by Eeyarestain I (Fiebiger et al., 2004) cause ER stress.
evidence: Supported by citation to pharmacological literature.

claim: Thapsigargin inhibits Ca2+ ATPase and causes ER stress.
source: The inhibition of N-linked glycosylation by Tunicamycin (Kuo and Lampen, 1974), Ca2+ ATPase by Thapsigargin (Lytton et al., 1991), proteasome by MG132 (Lee and Goldberg, 1998), and ERAD by Eeyarestain I (Fiebiger et al., 2004) cause ER stress.
evidence: Supported by citation to pharmacological literature.

claim: MG132 inhibits the proteasome and causes ER stress.
source: The inhibition of N-linked glycosylation by Tunicamycin (Kuo and Lampen, 1974), Ca2+ ATPase by Thapsigargin (Lytton et al., 1991), proteasome by MG132 (Lee and Goldberg, 1998), and ERAD by Eeyarestain I (Fiebiger et al., 2004) cause ER stress.
evidence: Supported by citation to pharmacological literature.

claim: Eeyarestatin I inhibits ERAD and causes ER stress.
source: The inhibition of N-linked glycosylation by Tunicamycin (Kuo and Lampen, 1974), Ca2+ ATPase by Thapsigargin (Lytton et al., 1991), proteasome by MG132 (Lee and Goldberg, 1998), and ERAD by Eeyarestain I (Fiebiger et al., 2004) cause ER stress.
evidence: Supported by citation to pharmacological literature.

claim: Addition of Tunicamycin, MG132, or Eeyarestatin I to fly food results in enhancement of Tsc1 knockdown eye size.
source: Addition of these small molecule inhibitors to the fly food, except Thapsigargin, resulted in an enhancement of Tsc1 knockdown eye size (Figure 3E), consistent with a regulation of Tsc1-deficient growth by the ER stress response status.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological treatment data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Tsc1-deficient growth is regulated by ER stress response status.
source: Addition of these small molecule inhibitors to the fly food, except Thapsigargin, resulted in an enhancement of Tsc1 knockdown eye size (Figure 3E), consistent with a regulation of Tsc1-deficient growth by the ER stress response status.
evidence: Inferred from the consistent effects of ER stress induction on Tsc1 mutant growth.

claim: Calnexin staining is stronger in Tsc1 and Tsc1 foxo mutant clones compared to surrounding wild-type tissue.
source: The staining was stronger in Tsc1 and Tsc1 foxo mutant clones as compared to the surrounding wild-type tissue, suggesting an upregulation of Cnx99A levels or a change in ER morphology in these cells.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Stronger calnexin staining in Tsc1 mutant clones suggests an upregulation of Cnx99A levels or a change in ER morphology.
source: The staining was stronger in Tsc1 and Tsc1 foxo mutant clones as compared to the surrounding wild-type tissue, suggesting an upregulation of Cnx99A levels or a change in ER morphology in these cells.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the immunofluorescence data.

claim: Increased ER stress in Tsc1 loss-of-function cells has been established.
source: Increased ER stress in Tsc1 loss-of-function cells has been established (Ozcan et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Hsc-70–3 transcript levels are elevated in Tsc1 foxo mutant eye imaginal discs compared to Tsc1 mutant discs.
source: RT-qPCR analysis of Tsc1 or Tsc1 foxo mutant eye imaginal discs dissected from larvae raised under normal food or NR showed elevated Hsc-70–3 transcript levels upon foxo loss (Figure 4B), indicating an enhancement of ER stress.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Elevated Hsc-70–3 transcript levels upon foxo loss indicate an enhancement of ER stress.
source: RT-qPCR analysis of Tsc1 or Tsc1 foxo mutant eye imaginal discs dissected from larvae raised under normal food or NR showed elevated Hsc-70–3 transcript levels upon foxo loss (Figure 4B), indicating an enhancement of ER stress.
evidence: Inferred from the known role of Hsc-70–3 as an ER stress reporter.

claim: PEK transcript levels are not changed upon foxo loss in Tsc1 mutant eye discs.
source: PEK transcript levels were not changed upon foxo loss in Tsc1 mutant eye discs (Figure 4B').
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4B'.

claim: PEK and Ire1 are the two conserved UPR branches in Drosophila.
source: Induction of UPR was also checked by analyzing the two conserved branches in Drosophila: PEK (PERK) and Ire1 (Mori, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on Drosophila UPR.

claim: Ire1 signals via splicing of the transcription factor X-box binding protein 1 (Xbp1).
source: Ire1 signals via splicing of the transcription factor X-box binding protein 1 (Xbp1) (Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on Ire1 signaling.

claim: Expression levels of spliced-Xbp1 are significantly increased in Tsc1 foxo mutant eye discs, specifically under conditions of nutrient restriction.
source: The expression levels of spliced-Xbp1 were significantly increased in Tsc1 foxo mutant eye discs, specifically under conditions of NR (Figure 4B'').
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4B''.

claim: Enrichment of spliced-Xbp1 in Tsc1 foxo knockdown clones under nutrient restriction is confirmed using an in vivo reporter.
source: The enrichment of spliced-Xbp1 was further confirmed in Tsc1 foxo knockdown clones under NR using an in vivo reporter (Sone et al., 2013; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: FoxO has the capacity to regulate ER stress status in Tsc1 mutant cells.
source: This illustrates the capacity of FoxO to regulate the ER stress status in Tsc1 mutant cells.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results showing FoxO's effect on ER stress markers.

claim: The majority of genes differentially upregulated in Tsc1 mutant cells upon foxo knockdown consist of snoRNAs and snRNAs.
source: The majority of the genes differentially upregulated in Tsc1 mutant cells upon foxo knockdown consisted of snoRNAs and snRNAs.
evidence: Supported by analysis of the RNA-seq data.

claim: snoRNAs function primarily in posttranscriptional modification of ribosomal RNAs and snRNAs to regulate ribosome biogenesis and function, RNA editing, gene silencing, and alternative splicing.
source: snoRNAs are single-stranded non-coding RNAs that function primarily in the posttranscriptional modification of ribosomal RNAs and snRNAs to regulate ribosome biogenesis and function, RNA editing, gene silencing, and alternative splicing (Bratkovič and Rogelj, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to review literature on snoRNA function.

claim: snoRNA genes are directly bound and activated by Myc in Drosophila S2 cells.
source: snoRNA genes were shown to be directly bound and activated by Myc in Drosophila S2 cells (Herter et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: The expression of myc is suppressed by FoxO in Drosophila muscles.
source: On the other hand, the expression of myc is suppressed by FoxO, at least in Drosophila muscles (Teleman et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: mTORC1 regulates Myc activity by controlling the amount of protein bound to promoters of target genes.
source: The same study reported that mTORC1 regulates Myc activity by controlling the amount of protein bound to promoters of target genes.
evidence: Supported by citation to the same study mentioned previously.

claim: Upon knockdown of foxo, the inhibition of myc expression by FoxO is alleviated under nutrient restriction, and Myc gets activated downstream of hyperactive mTORC1.
source: A similar mechanism might be at play in the Tsc1 mutant cells of the eye imaginal discs. Upon knockdown of foxo, the inhibition of myc expression by FoxO is alleviated under NR, and Myc gets activated downstream of hyperactive mTORC1.
evidence: Speculative mechanistic interpretation based on prior literature and current findings.

claim: Myc activation can lead to upregulation of snoRNAs, which helps in biomass production in rapidly growing cells.
source: This can lead to a subsequent upregulation of snoRNAs, which helps in biomass production in these rapidly growing cells.
evidence: Speculative mechanistic interpretation based on known Myc function.

claim: Emerging evidence suggests a correlation between snoRNAs and sustained proliferation, invasion, metastasis, and angiogenesis in different cancers.
source: Indeed, emerging evidence suggests a correlation between snoRNAs and sustained proliferation, invasion, metastasis, and angiogenesis in different cancers (Liang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to review literature on snoRNAs in cancer.

claim: There is significant interplay between the PI3K/Akt/mTORC1 signaling network and ER stress pathways.
source: There is a significant interplay between the PI3K/Akt/mTORC1 signaling network and ER stress pathways (Appenzeller-Herzog and Hall, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to review literature.

claim: Induction of ER stress results in suppression of insulin receptor signaling linking ER stress to insulin resistance.
source: Induction of ER stress results in the suppression of insulin receptor signaling linking ER stress to insulin resistance (Ozcan et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: PEK-driven regulation of FoxO contributes to insulin resistance in Drosophila.
source: Similarly, PEK-driven regulation of FoxO contributes to this resistance in Drosophila (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study in Drosophila.

claim: Uncontrolled activation of Akt represses ER stress in cardiac dysfunction.
source: In a study on cardiac dysfunction, uncontrolled activation of Akt repressed ER stress (Dong et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: Hyperactivation of mTORC1 activity via loss of TSC complex function leads to increased ER stress and UPR pathway upregulation.
source: Hyperactivation of mTORC1 activity, particularly via loss of the TSC complex function, leads to increased ER stress and UPR pathway upregulation (Ozcan et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: ER stress inhibits Akt and mTORC1 activity to induce autophagy.
source: In turn, ER stress inhibits Akt and mTORC1 activity to induce autophagy (Qin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: The identification of putative ERAD components governing Tsc1 mutant tissue growth adds another interaction node to the PI3K/Akt/mTORC1 and ER stress pathway crosstalk.
source: Our identification of putative ERAD components governing Tsc1 mutant tissue growth adds another interaction node to this pathway crosstalk.
evidence: Inferred from the novel findings in the context of existing pathway knowledge.

claim: The absence of canonical ERAD components in the transcriptomics data prompted consideration of an independent mechanism for degradation of misfolded proteins.
source: The absence of canonical ERAD components in the transcriptomics data prompted us to consider the possibility of an independent mechanism for the degradation of misfolded proteins, as shown previously in C. elegans (Safra et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the data and prior literature in C. elegans.

claim: Enhancement of Tsc1 loss-of-function overgrowth upon downregulation of core ERAD components implies an important role of the Hrd3-E3 ubiquitin ligase complex in this growth process.
source: However, enhancement of the Tsc1 loss-of-function overgrowth upon downregulation of the core ERAD components implies an important role of the Hrd3-E3 ubiquitin ligase complex in this growth process.
evidence: Inferred from the genetic screening results.

claim: FoxO restricts Tsc1 mutant tissue growth at the level of proliferation.
source: Given that FoxO restricts Tsc1 mutant tissue growth at the level of proliferation, a lack of known proliferation-affecting genes among the differentially regulated genes is intriguing.
evidence: Based on prior characterization of FoxO function.

claim: The inhibitory effect on proliferation by FoxO might be indirect, possibly via ER stress response pathways.
source: This suggests that the inhibitory effect on proliferation by FoxO might be indirect, possibly via ER stress response pathways (Vandewynckel et al., 2013).
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the data and cited literature.

claim: PERK reduces oxidative DNA damage and checkpoint activation to increase proliferation of cancer cells.
source: PERK reduces oxidative DNA damage and checkpoint activation to increase proliferation of cancer cells (Bobrovnikova-Marjon et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: GRP78 plays a role in regulating tumor cell proliferation by various means.
source: A role for the ER chaperone GRP78 in regulating tumor cell proliferation by various means has also been described (Lee, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to review literature.

claim: IRE1α promotes cell proliferation by regulating expression of cyclin A1 through XBP-1 splicing.
source: IRE1α has been shown to promote cell proliferation by regulating expression of cyclin A1 through XBP-1 splicing (Thorpe and Schwarze, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: Heightened expression of Hsc-70–3 and spliced-Xbp1 in Tsc1 mutant cells upon foxo loss under nutrient restriction hints at a possible approach to reinforce proliferation in these cells.
source: Our results indeed demonstrate a heightened expression of Hsc-70–3 and spliced-Xbp1 in Tsc1 mutant cells upon foxo loss under NR, hinting at a possible approach to reinforce proliferation in these cells.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: PEK might be regulated at a level other than transcription.
source: PEK might also be regulated at a level other than transcription.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the lack of transcriptional changes observed.

claim: Aberrant ER stress activation has been recorded during various aspects of cancer development.
source: Aberrant ER stress activation has also been recorded during various aspects of cancer development (Avril et al., 2017; Wang and Kaufman, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to review literature on ER stress in cancer.

claim: Considerable efforts have been made to develop therapeutic strategies to target tumor cell dependency on ER stress response pathways or to substantially upregulate stress to cause cell death.
source: Considerable efforts have been made to develop therapeutic strategies to target the dependency of tumor cells on ER stress response pathways, or to substantially upregulate stress to cause cell death (Hetz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to review literature on therapeutic strategies.

claim: Use of ER stress-inducing agents has displayed sensitization of Tsc1/2 mutant cells to individual treatments in vitro.
source: Specifically, in the case of loss of Tsc1/2 function, use of ER stress-inducing agents has displayed sensitization of mutant cells to individual treatments in vitro (Kang et al., 2011), or combination treatments in a mouse xenograft tumor model (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Use of ER stress-inducing agents has displayed sensitization of Tsc1/2 mutant cells to combination treatments in a mouse xenograft tumor model.
source: Specifically, in the case of loss of Tsc1/2 function, use of ER stress-inducing agents has displayed sensitization of mutant cells to individual treatments in vitro (Kang et al., 2011), or combination treatments in a mouse xenograft tumor model (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The ER stress response can have both pro-survival and pro-apoptotic effects.
source: Since the ER stress response can have both pro-survival and pro-apoptotic effects (Ma and Hendershot, 2004), it is crucial to characterize the signaling landscape of individual tumors before therapeutic intervention.
evidence: Supported by citation to review literature on ER stress responses.

claim: It is crucial to characterize the signaling landscape of individual tumors before therapeutic intervention targeting ER stress.
source: Since the ER stress response can have both pro-survival and pro-apoptotic effects (Ma and Hendershot, 2004), it is crucial to characterize the signaling landscape of individual tumors before therapeutic intervention.
evidence: Inferred from the dual nature of ER stress responses and clinical implications.

claim: Increasing ER stress leads to enhancement of Tsc1 mutant overgrowth.
source: For instance, our results demonstrate that increasing ER stress led to an enhancement of Tsc1 mutant overgrowth.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Suppression of foxo represses ERAD pathway activation in Tsc1 mutant cells.
source: Suppression of foxo represses the ERAD pathway activation, which combined with the augmented protein synthesis in Tsc1 mutant cells results in a state of high ER stress.
evidence: Inferred from the transcriptomics and functional data presented.

claim: Suppression of foxo combined with augmented protein synthesis in Tsc1 mutant cells results in a state of high ER stress.
source: Suppression of foxo represses the ERAD pathway activation, which combined with the augmented protein synthesis in Tsc1 mutant cells results in a state of high ER stress.
evidence: Inferred from the combined effects of foxo loss and Tsc1 mutation.

claim: High ER stress state is beneficial for proliferation and confers a growth advantage to Tsc1 foxo mutant cells.
source: This new adaptive state is beneficial for proliferation and confers a growth advantage to Tsc1 foxo mutant cells.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the observed overgrowth phenotype.

claim: Exploitation of ER stress processes in tumors with escalated mTORC1 activity that exhibit loss of FoxOs can extend the repertoire of available treatment options.
source: The exploitation of this process in tumors with escalated mTORC1 activity that exhibit loss of FoxOs can extend the repertoire of available treatment options and needs further exploration.
evidence: Speculative proposal for therapeutic application based on the findings.

claim: High variability among biological replicates in the RNA-seq data can be explained by small starting material for library preparation and absence of pooling of multiple samples.
source: Clustering on normalized gene counts showed high variability among the biological replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). This can be explained by the small starting material for library preparation (Bhargava et al., 2015) and an absence of pooling of multiple samples to average the individual organismal differences.
evidence: Inferred from technical considerations and cited literature on LCM-based RNA-seq.

claim: A reduction in foxo transcripts was not observed in the knockdown samples.
source: Interestingly, a reduction in foxo transcripts was not observed in the knockdown samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Partial loss of foxo transcripts accompanied by significant loss of protein suggests the presence of a transcriptionally-activating feedback upon foxo knockdown or a direct effect on translational capacity.
source: A similar partial loss of transcripts accompanied by a significant loss of protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) was observed in Kc167 cells, suggesting the presence of a transcriptionally-activating feedback upon foxo knockdown or a direct effect on the translational capacity (Doench et al., 2003).
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the discrepancy between transcript and protein levels, with citation to relevant literature.

claim: Processed cell populations were not contaminated with GFP-positive non-clonal tissue.
source: Representative images of isolated Tsc1 mutant clones with and without foxo knockdown are presented to support that the processed cell populations were not contaminated with GFP-positive non-clonal tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 100% mutant transcripts (Tsc1Q87X) are present in the Tsc1 mutant clones.
source: This is further substantiated by the presence of 100% mutant transcripts (Tsc1Q87X where codon CAG at position 3R:24,130,984 is substituted by TAG) in the Tsc1 mutant clones (example in Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: GSEA showed enrichment of genes upregulated in Tsc1 mutant discs in corresponding lists of differentially expressed genes.
source: Finally, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Subramanian et al., 2005) showed enrichment of genes upregulated in Tsc1 mutant discs (Harvey et al., 2008) as well as FoxO targets from adipose tissue and muscle (Teleman et al., 2008) in corresponding lists of differentially expressed genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: GSEA showed enrichment of FoxO targets from adipose tissue and muscle in corresponding lists of differentially expressed genes.
source: Finally, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Subramanian et al., 2005) showed enrichment of genes upregulated in Tsc1 mutant discs (Harvey et al., 2008) as well as FoxO targets from adipose tissue and muscle (Teleman et al., 2008) in corresponding lists of differentially expressed genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Calnexin is an ER molecular chaperone and a Ca2+ homeostasis regulator.
source: Calnexin is an ER molecular chaperone and a Ca2+ homeostasis regulator (Arruda and Hotamisligil, 2015) that is localized to the ER membrane (Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on calnexin function.

claim: Calnexin is localized to the ER membrane.
source: Calnexin is an ER molecular chaperone and a Ca2+ homeostasis regulator (Arruda and Hotamisligil, 2015) that is localized to the ER membrane (Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on calnexin localization.

claim: This is the first report illustrating the use of laser capture microdissection with living imaginal disc cells in Drosophila that was not based on pooling of multiple biological samples.
source: Earlier studies (Mauthner et al., 2014; Spletter et al., 2007) have described the use of LCM for RNA isolation from optimal cutting temperature compound-embedded tissues, but this is the first report, to our knowledge, illustrating the use of this technique with living imaginal disc cells in Drosophila that was not based on pooling of multiple biological samples.
evidence: Based on the authors' assessment of the literature and their methodological innovation.
